results.input: 1. van den Hoek et al. Normative data for squat, bench press and deadlift exercises in powerlifting: Data from 809,986 competition entries. Suggested use: raw unequipped drug-tested competition SBD relative strength.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: sex, age at competition, body mass at competition, maximum successful squat, maximum successful bench press, maximum successful deadlift, unequipped status, drug-tested competition status, competition federation/rules, competition date
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Data were taken from sanctioned drug-tested, unequipped competitions. Maximum successful lift and body mass at that competition were extracted; each lift was normalized as maximum lift in kg divided by athlete body mass in kg. Technical rules could vary slightly by federation; typical successful-lift requirements are summarized by the authors.
output.exercise_or_test: Maximum successful competition squat, bench press, and deadlift attempts; competition-style relative 1RM strength.
output.permitted_use_note: The article is open access under CC BY 4.0, but the underlying competition records were sourced from OpenPowerlifting and may carry separate database or attribution conditions; verify both licenses and preserve source attribution before importing or redistributing numeric norms.
output.population_and_sample: Retrospective global competition-record analysis of 809,986 entries from drug-tested, unequipped powerlifting competitions held from 1968–2022 across Africa, Asia, Europe, the Americas, and Oceania; 571,650 male and 238,336 female entries, ages 12–96 years. Entries may represent the same athlete more than once; mean age was 30.5 ± 13.3 years and mean body mass 82.4 ± 21.3 kg.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Relative-strength norms were reported by sex, United Nations age categories (12–17, 18–35, 36–59, 60–79, and 80+ years), current IPF weight class, and combined age/weight class, using deciles from the 10th through 90th percentiles with 95% confidence intervals; small cells (n<20) were reported as median with 95% CI.
output.verified_citation: Daniel J. van den Hoek, Patrick L. Beaumont, Adele K. van den Hoek, Patrick J. Owen, Joel M. Garrett, Robert Buhmann, Christopher Latella (2024). Normative data for the squat, bench press and deadlift exercises in powerlifting: Data from 809,986 competition entries. DOI: 10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.005; PMID: 39060209.

results.input: 2. Prado et al. Reference Values for Maximal Strength in Elite Judo Athletes: National- and International-Level Competitors. Suggested tests: back squat, bench press, prone row.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: sex, age, sport, competitive level, weight category, body mass, test name, 1RM absolute load, relative-strength calculation, protocol/equipment details
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: The authoritative abstract verifies 1RM testing and reports absolute and relative-strength analyses, but does not provide the detailed execution protocol, equipment, range-of-motion standards, warm-up/loading sequence, reliability criteria, or exact body-mass normalization formula; these must be verified from the full article before matching.
output.exercise_or_test: One-repetition maximum (1RM) back squat, bench press, and prone row.
output.permitted_use_note: The publisher page indicates the full article and numeric content require access or purchase; use numeric tables only after confirming lawful access/licensing and the complete protocol, and do not reproduce restricted tables without permission.
output.population_and_sample: 112 elite judo athletes (68 males, 44 females) competing at national and international levels; the authoritative abstract does not verify age range, participant geography, or the detailed distribution by sex, weight category, and competitive level.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Percentile-based classification tables were developed; analyses/stratification reported by sex, weight category, and competitive level (national versus international), with absolute and relative strength outcomes. Numeric percentile cut points and tables were not available in the authoritative abstract.
output.verified_citation: Campos BT, Abad CCC, Penna EM, Lima COV, Avelar AF, de Rezende CM, da Silveira-Rodrigues JG, Prado LS (2026). Reference Values for Maximal Strength in Elite Judo Athletes: National- and International-Level Competitors. DOI: 10.1080/02701367.2026.2636255; PMID: 41996598.

results.input: 3. Lesinski et al. Maturation-, age-, and sex-specific anthropometric and physical fitness percentiles of German elite young athletes.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: test name and version, raw result and units, test date/age, sex, standing height, sitting height, leg length, body mass, calculated maturity offset/status, sport context, equipment/protocol metadata
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: The article states that testing was performed under strictly standardized conditions and reports the named tests, but a comparison must verify the same test versions, equipment, trial/scoring rules, units, and whether any outcome is absolute or body-size normalized; maturity status was derived from Mirwald peak-height-velocity equations using age, standing height, sitting height, leg length, and body mass, then classified as pre-pubertal (<−1 year from PHV), pubertal (±1 year), or post-pubertal (>1 year).
output.exercise_or_test: Standing and sitting body height, body mass, body-mass index, countermovement jump, drop jump, change-of-direction speed (T-test), trunk-muscle endurance (ventral Bourban test), dynamic lower-limb balance (Y-balance test), and hand-grip strength.
output.permitted_use_note: The publisher and institutional record identify the article as open access under CC BY 4.0, subject to attribution and the license terms; numeric reuse should preserve the study’s cohort definition, citation, stratification, and exact protocol, and should not be presented as a universal or causal norm.
output.population_and_sample: Cross-sectional convenience sample of 703 German elite young athletes (420 male, 283 female), aged 8–18 years, from 18 sports, recruited from German elite sport schools; athletes completed at least 10 hours of training per week and had practiced their sport for approximately 2–12 years.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Reference values are percentile distributions for anthropometric and physical-fitness outcomes stratified by chronological age, sex, and maturation status; the study covers elite youth athletes across multiple sports rather than a single sport or strength-only cohort.
output.verified_citation: Lesinski M, Schmelcher A, Herz M, Puta C, Gabriel H, Arampatzis A, Laube G, Büsch D, Granacher U (2020). Maturation-, age-, and sex-specific anthropometric and physical fitness percentiles of German elite young athletes. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0237423; PMID: 32790710.

results.input: 4. Eriksrud et al. NHANES analysis: Reference Curves for Field Tests of Musculoskeletal Fitness in U.S. Children and Adolescents: 2012 NHANES National Youth Fitness Survey.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, test name, test variant, raw score, units, protocol/equipment, test date or age at test, body mass, height, normalization method
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: The PubMed record confirms the named tests and the relative/allometrically scaled handgrip variants, but does not provide the complete equipment, positioning, cadence, timing, scoring, or scaling equations. Any comparison therefore requires retrieval and exact matching of the article’s full methods; body-size normalization is relevant for the relative and allometrically scaled handgrip outputs, while absolute handgrip is unnormalized.
output.exercise_or_test: Handgrip strength (absolute, relative, and allometrically scaled), modified pull-ups, and plank test.
output.permitted_use_note: Use the PubMed-verified publication as the bibliographic authority and treat numeric curves/tables as publication-derived data subject to the publisher’s access and reuse terms; the restricted NNYFS microdata require authorized access, proposal approval, confidentiality training, and a data-use agreement.
output.population_and_sample: Nationally representative U.S. National Youth Fitness Survey participants aged 3–15 years; 1,453 participants were tested on musculoskeletal fitness in the publication, while the CDC survey record reports 1,640 interviewed and 1,576 examined. The survey was conducted in 2012 through household interviews and mobile examination-center testing; no athlete-only or training-specific sample was established.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Age-specific and sex-specific smoothed percentile growth curves were created using LMS regression for the musculoskeletal-fitness measures; the article also used existing age- and sex-specific percentiles to assign z-scores for aerobic capacity and body composition. The accessible record does not expose the numeric curve tables or all percentile values.
output.verified_citation: Kelly R. Laurson, Pedro F. Saint-Maurice, Gregory J. Welk, and Joey C. Eisenmann (2017). Reference Curves for Field Tests of Musculoskeletal Fitness in U.S. Children and Adolescents: The 2012 NHANES National Youth Fitness Survey. DOI: 10.1519/JSC.0000000000001678; PMID: 27741055.

results.input: 5. FitBack consortium: European fitness landscape for children and adolescents. Suggested tests: handgrip and standing long jump.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: test name, raw score, test units, test date/age, sex, country/geography, protocol/equipment, hand tested (for handgrip), body height, body mass, BMI/waist circumference if used for any normalization, training/sport context
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Standing long jump: toes behind a start line, feet shoulder-width apart, jump and land with feet together, two attempts, best distance recorded to the nearest centimetre. Handgrip: adjustable-grip hand dynamometer (e.g., TKK 5101 Grip D), handle set to hand size, elbow fully extended, gradual continuous squeeze for at least 2 seconds, both hands tested twice alternately with short rest, best result recorded to 0.1 kg. The source also measures height, weight, BMI and waist circumference; no universal body-size normalization of handgrip or jump is stated in the verified summary, so raw scores must not be normalized or transformed without matching the source method.
output.exercise_or_test: Handgrip strength test and standing long jump test (ALPHA fitness battery muscular-strength tests).
output.permitted_use_note: The peer-reviewed article is open access and the FitBack platform is described as open access, but the platform carries its own terms and conditions and the source data are aggregated from many contributing datasets; use only the published/reference outputs and verify licensing before redistributing tables or embedding numeric norms commercially.
output.population_and_sample: European children and adolescents aged 6–18 years; 7,966,693 test results from 106 datasets across 34 countries, drawn from population fitness surveillance/monitoring and usable in school and/or sport settings; the article does not establish a single athlete-only cohort.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Sex-specific and age-specific percentile values for ages 6–18 were derived using generalized additive models for location, scale and shape; country-level rankings and mean percentiles are also reported. The verified source does not justify substituting athlete-specific or sport-specific norms.
output.verified_citation: Ortega FB, Leskošek B, Blagus R, et al. (2023). European fitness landscape for children and adolescents: updated reference values, fitness maps and country rankings based on nearly 8 million test results from 34 countries gathered by the FitBack network. DOI: 10.1136/bjsports-2022-106176; PMID: 36623866.

results.input: 6. IDEFICS: Physical fitness reference standards in European children. Suggested tests: handgrip and standing long jump.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, country/geography, handgrip dynamometer model, handgrip protocol and hand-size adjustment, handgrip result (kg), standing-long-jump protocol, standing-long-jump result (cm), height, weight
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Handgrip used a Takei TKK 5101 dynamometer; the child stood bipedally with arms fully extended, without the dynamometer touching the body, and the device was adjusted for sex and hand size. Standing long jump required a maximal jump from standing with a two-foot takeoff and landing with both feet together. Analytic inclusion required complete weight, height, age, and sex; the record does not establish a universal body-size-normalized score for these two tests.
output.exercise_or_test: Handgrip strength test; standing long jump test (lower-limb explosive strength).
output.permitted_use_note: Use the published reference tables/curves only for their stated pediatric European population and matching protocols; do not treat them as norms for trained athletes or reproduce numeric tables beyond applicable permission/licensing terms.
output.population_and_sample: 10,302 children aged 6–10.9 years (50.7% girls) from the IDEFICS multicentre study in eight European countries: Sweden, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Cyprus, Spain, Belgium, and Estonia; the analysis was cross-sectional and not an athlete-only sample.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Sex- and age-specific percentile curves were reported; percentiles were 1st, 3rd, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, 97th, and 99th. The paper reports handgrip in kilograms and standing long jump in centimetres, with test-specific sample sizes varying because participation was incomplete.
output.verified_citation: De Miguel-Etayo P, Gracia-Marco L, Ortega FB, Intemann T, Foraita R, Lissner L, Oja L, Barba G, Michels N, Tornaritis M, Molnár D, Pitsiladis Y, Ahrens W, Moreno LA; IDEFICS consortium (2014). Physical fitness reference standards in European children: the IDEFICS study. DOI: 10.1038/ijo.2014.136; PMID: 25376221.

results.input: 7. Chinese National Survey: Percentile Curves for Multiple Physical Fitness Components Among Chinese Han Children and Adolescents Aged 7–18.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, Han-ethnicity/reference-population eligibility, geography/school-population context, nutritional-status category or BMI-for-age Z-score, exact test name, raw result, units, protocol version, attempt count, and test-specific age/sex form
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Standardized field protocols: FVC spirometer, maximum of two attempts; standing long jump maximum of three, nearest 1 cm; 50-m dash timed to nearest 0.1 s; sit-and-reach maximum of two, nearest 0.1 cm; grip dynamometer maximum of two, nearest 0.1 kg; specified pull-up/sit-up/shuttle/run procedures. Height and weight were measured with calibrated equipment; BMI was weight/height² and normal weight was defined using WHO 2007 BMI-for-age Z-score criteria (thinness <−2 SD; overweight/obesity >+1 SD). No athlete-specific or strength-to-body-mass normalization was reported.
output.exercise_or_test: Forced vital capacity; standing long jump; 50-m dash; sit-and-reach; grip strength; body-muscle strength (oblique body pull-ups for boys 7–12, pull-ups for boys 13–18, 1-minute sit-ups for girls 7–18); endurance running (eight 50-m shuttle runs for ages 7–12, 1,000-m run for boys 13–18, 800-m run for girls 13–18).
output.permitted_use_note: The article is CC BY for attributed publication use, but the underlying individual de-identified survey data are restricted and may be shared only after proposed-use approval by an independent review committee via the corresponding authors; do not reproduce or infer unpublished individual-level norms.
output.population_and_sample: Cross-sectional 2014 Chinese National Survey on Students’ Constitution and Health: 214,228 Han children/adolescents aged 7–18 years (107,180 boys; 107,048 girls) from 26 provinces and four mainland municipalities, excluding Tibet, Hong Kong, Macau, and Taiwan; 161,999 were classified as normal weight. This is a general school-based population, not an athlete-trained cohort.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Sex- and age-specific percentile curves and tables for total and normal-weight populations; modeled percentiles P5, P10, P20, P30, P40, P50, P60, P70, P80, P90, and P95 using GAMLSS, with displayed curves emphasizing P20/P40/P60/P80. Pull-ups used observed-distribution nonparametric percentiles; subgroup sample sizes vary by test because not all participants completed every test.
output.verified_citation: Ma N, Dang J, Liu Y, Zhong P, Yan X, Zhang J, Dong Y, Song Y, Ma J, Lau PWC (2022). Percentile Curves for Multiple Physical Fitness Components Among Chinese Han Children and Adolescents Aged 7–18 Years From a National Survey Based on the Total and the Normal Weight Population. results.input: 8. Physical fitness reference standards for Chinese children and adolescents. Suggested tests: handgrip, standing long jump, 30-second sit-ups.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: test name/protocol, result and unit, age, sex, measurement date or age basis, China-relevant population/geography, body size (height and weight/BMI) for contextual review, youth/non-athlete status
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Grip strength: standing upright, feet shoulder-width apart, elbow fully extended, maximal squeeze continuously for at least 2 seconds, twice; larger value recorded. Standing long jump: take off and land with feet together; distance from start line to the nearest heel, twice; best score retained in centimeters. 30-second sit-ups: supine on a cushion, feet held by an assistant, hands crossed over chest; count repetitions in which the forehead touches the knee within 30 seconds. The paper reports age- and sex-specific raw performance standards; no body-size normalization is applied to these three test outputs, although height, weight, and BMI were recorded.
output.exercise_or_test: Grip strength; standing long jump; 30-second sit-ups; plus sit-and-reach, 50-m dash, 20-second repeated straddling, and 20-m shuttle-run test.
output.permitted_use_note: The PMC/publisher record identifies the article as open access; any reuse of numeric tables or derived displays should follow the article’s stated license/attribution terms and should not imply that a youth population reference is an athlete-performance norm.
output.population_and_sample: 85,535 Chinese children and adolescents aged 7–18 years (48.7% girls), recruited in 2015–2016 from public urban and rural schools across 27 provinces in six geographical divisions using stratified randomized cluster sampling; students with physical or mental disabilities were excluded, and 2.1% were from Lhasa/Tibet.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Age- and sex-specific percentile curves and percentile values were calculated with the LMS method for each test; the article also reports age/sex-stratified descriptive means and standard deviations. The reference dimensions are age 7–18 years and sex, with geography represented by the national multi-region sample rather than separate fully reported regional norms.
output.verified_citation: Feng Zhang, Cunjian Bi, Xiaojian Yin, Qi Chen, Yuqiang Li, Yuan Liu, Ting Zhang, Ming Li, Yi Sun, and Xiaofang Yang (2021). Physical fitness reference standards for Chinese children and adolescents. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-021-84634-7; PMID: 33654251.

results.input: 9. MoMo Study: Representative Percentile Curves of Physical Fitness From Early Childhood to Early Adulthood. Suggested tests: push-ups, sit-ups, standing long jump.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, country/reference population, test name, exact protocol/version, standing-long-jump best valid distance or push-up/sit-up valid repetitions in 40 seconds, test date or wave, body size if collected for audit (not established as a normalization variable)
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Standing long jump: jump from a marker on a tartan granulate mat with both legs and no backward fall; two valid attempts are evaluated. Push-ups: not administered to 4–5-year-olds; clean repetitions with arms extended, only hands and feet contacting the floor, hands briefly brought together behind the buttocks in the ground position and one hand touching the other in support; 40 seconds, counting correct repetitions. Sit-ups: not suitable up to age 5; supine with knees bent and feet fixed, fingertips at temples, elbows touch knees at the top, shoulder blades touch the mat on lowering, pelvis stays on the floor; 40 seconds, counting valid repetitions. The source specifies age/sex standardization but does not establish body-size normalization for these three outcomes; raw test results and exact execution must match the MoMo manual.
output.exercise_or_test: MoMo Motor Performance Test items: standing long jump, push-ups, and sit-ups; the full profile also included ergometric endurance testing, jumping side-ways, balancing backwards, static stand, and stand-and-reach.
output.permitted_use_note: Use only as a population reference with exact MoMo protocol and age/sex scope; do not present it as athlete-performance norms or extrapolate beyond Germany ages 4–17. The article is openly available through PMC under the publisher's stated license, but the underlying participant-level data and the separate test manual should not be redistributed or reused beyond their terms.
output.population_and_sample: Nationwide representative Motorik-Modul (MoMo) Study, Germany, Wave 1 (2009–2012): 3,742 participants aged 4–23 years, 50.1% female; the reported representative percentile reference scope is ages 4–17 years (3,284 children/adolescents), and the sample is not representative after age 17. The cohort is population-based, not an athlete-trained or sport-specific sample.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: LMS-derived, standardized age- and sex-specific percentile curves for the eight test items; representative reporting is for Germany ages 4–17, with age and sex as the principal stratification dimensions. The article does not provide a sport-athlete norm set.
output.verified_citation: Claudia Niessner, Till Utesch, Doris Oriwol, Anke Hanssen-Doose, Steffen C. E. Schmidt, Alexander Woll, Klaus Bös, and Annette Worth (2020). Representative Percentile Curves of Physical Fitness From Early Childhood to Early Adulthood: The MoMo Study. DOI: 10.3389/fpubh.2020.00458; PMID: 33014968.

results.input: 10. COMO/DigiMot Study: Reference percentiles for children and adolescents for the digital motor performance test. Suggested tests: push-ups and sit-ups.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, country/population context, test name, remote-videoconference administration, 40-second duration, one trial, repetition count, standardized mat/setup, test date or age at assessment
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Videoconference-administered test using a standardized non-slip foldable mat (183 × 61 × 0.4 cm); one trial for Push-ups and one trial for Sit-ups, with synchronized timing and optional recording for quality assurance. The study collected body height, weight, and BMI, but the reported percentile curves are stratified by age and sex rather than presented as BMI- or height-normalized scores.
output.exercise_or_test: DigiMot Push-ups and Sit-ups; each is a remotely administered muscular-endurance test performed for 40 seconds.
output.permitted_use_note: The source is available through PubMed Central and links to the Scientific Reports publisher record; use only the published DigiMot protocol and reference curves, preserve the German non-athlete reference-population boundary, and check the article's license/any publisher restrictions before redistributing extracted numeric tables.
output.population_and_sample: German children and adolescents participating in the population-based COMO-1 DigiMot substudy; 1,149 participants aged 7–17 years (554 male, 595 female; mean age 11.4 ± 2.8 years). The published reference curves are presented for ages 7–15 years, with sparse older-age cells; participants were not selected as athletes.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Age- and sex-specific percentile curves generated with generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape; separate reference distributions are provided for boys and girls, with published figures covering ages 7–15 years. Exact percentile values must be taken from the article's tables/curves and must not be inferred from the abstract.
output.verified_citation: Klein T, Worth A, Niessner C, Merk S, Hanssen-Doose A (2026). Reference percentiles for children and adolescents for the digital motor performance test (DigiMot): results from the COMO-study. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-40270-7; PMID: 41699020.

results.input: 11. Korean National Fitness Award Project: Physical Fitness Levels in Korean Adolescents. Suggested tests: handgrip and partial curl-up.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: test name, test protocol, score and units, age, sex, country/population, test date or reference era, handgrip measurement side/selection rule, body mass if requesting a normalized comparison
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Certified professional instructors administered the tests. Handgrip strength was measured twice for each hand and the highest value recorded to the nearest 0.1 kg; partial curl-up performance was the maximum repetitions completed at the beep. The reported handgrip reference is absolute strength in kg; no body-size normalization was specified for these reference curves.
output.exercise_or_test: Handgrip strength test; partial curl-up test (also assessed in the battery were the 20-m PACER, 30-s endurance jump, and sit-and-reach test).
output.permitted_use_note: Use only for narrowly matched Korean adolescent reference comparisons and respect the journal/PMC copyright and reuse terms; do not present these norms as athlete-specific or generalize beyond the stated age, sex, geography, tests, and protocol.
output.population_and_sample: 14,794 Korean adolescents aged 13–18 years (7,688 boys and 7,106 girls) participating in the National Fitness Award Project in 2013–2014; the dataset combined preliminary random samples from 10 regions with voluntary main-project participants, and was not an athlete-only sample.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Age- and sex-specific smoothed LMS percentile curves for ages 13–18, with the 5th, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th, and 95th percentiles; handgrip and partial curl-up results are stratified by age and sex.
output.verified_citation: Lee S, Ko BG, Park S (2017). Physical Fitness Levels in Korean Adolescents: The National Fitness Award Project. DOI: 10.7570/jomes.2017.26.1.61; PMID: 31089495.

results.input: 12. FUPRECOL: Normative Reference Values for Handgrip Strength in Colombian Schoolchildren.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, geography/population eligibility, handgrip value, dynamometer model and grip/procedure details, test date or age at test; body mass and height if using any relative or body-size-normalized comparison
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: The accessible authoritative record verifies only an adjustable-grip hand dynamometer; it does not specify the manufacturer/model, posture, hand-selection rule, number of trials, rest interval, scoring rule, or exact body-size normalization. Do not infer these details. The abstract refers to combined HG for Health Benefit Zones and reports sex- and age-specific standards.

output.permitted_use_note: The PubMed record confirms the study and its published reference framework, but the numeric tables and full protocol are publisher-controlled through Wolters Kluwer; obtain and review the full article and licensing terms before reproducing numeric percentiles or embedding them in a commercial product.

No athlete-training cohort is identified in the PubMed record.

output.verified_citation: Ramírez-Vélez R, Morales O, Peña-Ibagon JC, Palacios-López A, Prieto-Benavides DH, Vivas A, Correa-Bautista JE, Lobelo F, Alonso-Martínez AM, Izquierdo M (2017). Normative Reference Values for Handgrip Strength in Colombian Schoolchildren: The FUPRECOL Study. DOI: 10.1519/JSC.0000000000001459; PMID: 27135472.

results.input: 13. Colombian youth study: Normative values for handgrip strength in Colombian children and adolescents from 6 to 17 years, including relative handgrip strength.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, country/geography, handgrip dynamometer model, handle adjustment/hand size, body position, arm/shoulder position, trial duration, number of trials per hand, valid-score rule (mean versus maximum), body weight, optional BMI, optional stature
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Takei TKK 5101 digital dynamometer with adjustable handle, 5–100 kg range and 0.1 kg precision. Participant stood bipedally with shoulder adducted and neutrally rotated, arm extended perpendicular to the body without contact, feet hip-width apart; handle was adjusted to hand size. Two or three 3–5-second maximal trials were performed per upper limb, and the highest score for each hand was valid. Normative HS used either the mean or maximum valid measurement per subject. HSRelative was HS divided by body weight in kilograms; supplementary estimates adjusted HS by BMI and stature. Body mass was measured barefoot in light clothing with a SECA 874 scale.
output.exercise_or_test: Handgrip strength (HS) measured separately in each upper limb; relative handgrip strength (HSRelative) was also evaluated.
output.permitted_use_note: The record is openly available through PubMed Central/SciELO, but numerical reuse should follow the article’s stated access/license terms and attribution requirements; the source is a national youth reference sample, not an athlete-performance norm, and its methods warn that differing dynamometers, positions, trial rules, and estimation methods can materially affect comparisons.
output.population_and_sample: Analytical cross-sectional secondary analysis of Colombia’s ENSIN-2015 national survey: 2,647 noninstitutional civilian children and adolescents, 6–17.9 years, permanent household residents across Colombia; 1,575 male and 1,072 female participants. Training or athlete status was not assessed, and physical-activity levels were not included in the centile values.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Sex- and age-specific quantile-regression reference values for absolute HS and weight-normalized HSRelative, using P5, P10, P25, P50, P75, P90, and P95; models were independently developed by sex and adjusted for the survey expansion factor. Tables provide mean-value and maximum-value variants; 98 weight observations were missing for analyses requiring weight.
output.verified_citation: Martínez-Torres J, Gallo-Villegas JA, Aguirre-Acevedo DC (2022). Normative values for handgrip strength in Colombian children and adolescents from 6 to 17 years of age: estimation using quantile regression. DOI: 10.1016/j.jped.2022.02.004; PMID: 35487284.

results.input: 14. NHANES allometric handgrip study: How Should Youth Handgrip Strength be Normalized?

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, country/population comparability, handgrip dynamometer model, hand tested or maximum-irrespective-of-hand rule, hand-size adjustment, standing test position, number of trials per hand, rest interval, height, body mass
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Takei electronic hand dynamometer T.K.K.5401; hand-size adjustment, one submaximal practice trial, standing upright with feet hip-width apart, arm extended and hanging away from the body, maximal squeeze while exhaling; three trials per hand, alternating hands, with 60 seconds’ rest between measures on the same hand. The primary allometric normalization was HGS/(height² × body mass^0.333); if only one body-size measure is available, HGS/height² was recommended. Height, body mass, and waist circumference were measured, but all three could not be used together because of collinearity.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: test name and exact protocol/equipment, sport, sex, age or study age group, dominant/nondominant side where applicable, raw score and units, height/upper-limb length where normalization applies, injury/pain status, training frequency/level
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Participants supplied age, height, weight, sex, practice hours/level, and injury history. After standardized warm-up and two familiarization trials, tests were randomized; generally three repetitions were performed with the best score retained, one-minute rests between repetitions and five-minute rests between tests; PSET was performed last after 15 minutes’ recovery and was not repeated to limit fatigue. SAMBT and SSASPT were recorded as maximal distance in meters; MCKCUEST and ULRT as maximal repetitions/touches; PSET as time to exhaustion at 30 beats/min with a shoulder-height bar and compensatory-movement criteria; UQYBT distances were normalized to upper-limb length; M-AST dynamometer values were multiplied by upper-limb length to yield N·m. Exact equipment/load details from Appendix A must be matched before comparison.

output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: CKCUEST: push-up position with hands on tape targets, alternating cross-body touches as rapidly as possible for 15 seconds; one trial, score is total reaches. results.input: 40. Normative values for calf muscle strength-endurance in the general population assessed with the Calf Raise Application. Suggested test: single-leg heel raise.

output.athlete_fields_required_for_match: age, sex, height, body mass, BMI, physical activity level, tested leg/dominance, repetitions, total work, total vertical displacement, peak height, 10° incline-board barefoot protocol, metronome cadence, Calf Raise Application measurement
output.exact_protocol_and_normalization: Barefoot single-leg stance on a 10° incline board, knee fully extended and trunk erect, with optional fingertip wall support; heel raised maximally and returned to the board at 30 repetitions/minute using a 60-beats/minute metronome until predefined failure criteria. An iPad/iPhone recorded from the side at 30 cm (up to 50 cm for longer feet); a 2.5-cm sticker below the distal lateral malleolus was tracked by computer vision. Normative quantile-regression models incorporated relevant personal characteristics, including age, height, mass, BMI, sex, and physical-activity level; the article does not define a simple universal body-size normalization formula.
output.exercise_or_test: Single-leg Heel Rise Endurance Test (HRET), performed on both dominant and non-dominant legs and assessed with the validated Calf Raise Application.
output.permitted_use_note: The publisher record identifies the article as open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license; reuse should still retain attribution and comply with the license. The Calf Raise Application is developer-associated, so app/software terms and any underlying-data restrictions should be checked before redistribution or commercial integration.
output.population_and_sample: 500 adults aged 18–81 years recruited at Erasmus MC University Medical Centre (Netherlands) and the University of Leicester (United Kingdom); 55% were female and 88% participated in physical activities. Participants had no current or prior Achilles tendon symptoms, Achilles/ankle surgery, recent lower-limb immobilization, or specified systemic inflammatory/internal disease.
output.reference_fields_or_percentiles: Reference outcomes were repetition count, total work (J), total vertical displacement (cm), and peak height (cm), reported with medians (50th percentile) and 95% reference intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles), stratified/adjusted by personal characteristics and leg dominance. Abstract medians for dominant/non-dominant legs were 25/24 repetitions, 1374/1325 J total work, 192/186 cm displacement, and 9.3/9.6 cm peak height.
output.verified_citation: Tjerk SO Sleeswijk Visser, Seth O’Neill, Kim Hébert-Losier, Denise Eygendaal, and Robert-Jan de Vos (2025). Normative values for calf muscle strength-endurance in the general population assessed with the Calf Raise Application: A large international cross-sectional study.
